**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I saw the name *Elias Voss* carved into the oak door of the old bookshop, I knew it was a mistake. Not because the name itself was wrong—it was elegant, old-fashioned, the kind of name that belonged on a tombstone or the spine of a first-edition novel—but because I had never heard it before. And yet, the moment I read it, my fingers twitched as if the wood itself had called my name.

I was twenty-three, working as a barista in a café that smelled like stale coffee and regret. The bookshop, *The Last Chapter*, was across the street, its windows filled with dusty tomes and the faint hum of a record player playing something classical and mournful. I had walked past it a hundred times, never entering, never looking closer. But that day, the door seemed to pull me in like a magnet.

Inside, the air was thick with the scent of aged paper and something else—something sharper, like ozone before a storm. The shelves were arranged in no particular order, as if the books had been dropped there by a careless giant and left to settle. A man sat behind the counter, his back to me, his fingers tracing the spine of a leather-bound volume. He was tall, his dark hair streaked with silver, his posture rigid with age. When he turned, I saw his face: sharp cheekbones, a nose that had been broken at least once, and eyes the color of storm clouds.

“You’re not from around here,” he said, his voice like gravel underfoot.

“I’m not,” I admitted.

He extended a hand. “Elias Voss.”

I shook it. His grip was strong, almost bruising. “Lena.”

He studied me for a long moment, as if deciding whether I was worth the trouble. Then, with a sigh, he gestured to the shelves. “Help yourself. But don’t touch the red ones.”

“The red ones?”

“The ones with the red spines. They’re not for sale.”

I didn’t ask why. Some things were better left unspoken.

---

The first red book I found was called *The Hollow Man*. Its cover was cracked, the title peeling away like sunburnt skin. Inside, the pages were filled with sketches—sketches of faces I recognized. My face. Faces of people I had never met but felt like I had known forever. And in the margins, in a handwriting that wasn’t mine, were words:

*You will remember. You will forget. You will remember again.*

I closed the book quickly, as if it might bite me.

Elias watched me from across the room, his expression unreadable. “You found one.”

“How did you—?”

“You have the look of someone who’s been looking for something they don’t want to find.”

I wanted to argue, but the words died in my throat.

---

The next day, I returned. And the next. Elias never asked why I came back. He just nodded at me, poured me a cup of tea from a pot that had seen better days, and let me wander the shelves. The red books were always there, waiting. Some had titles I recognized—*The Weight of Names*, *The Language of Shadows*, *The Thing That Loves You Back*. Others had no titles at all, just blank pages or symbols that made my skin crawl.

One evening, as the sun set outside, painting the windows in gold and crimson, I found a book with my name on the spine. *Lena Kovalic*. It was a journal, its pages filled with my handwriting—entries I didn’t remember writing. The first one was dated three years ago, the day I had moved to the city. I had written about the fear of being forgotten, of becoming just another face in the crowd. The last entry was from last week, the day before I had met Elias. I had written:

*They’re watching me. I can feel them. They want something.*

I slammed the book shut. My hands were shaking.

Elias appeared beside me, his breath warm against my ear. “You shouldn’t have touched that one.”

“I didn’t—”

“You did. And now you know.”

I turned to him, my voice raw. “What is this place? What are these books?”

He looked away, his jaw tightening. “Some things are better left unknown.”

“Bullshit.”

A long silence. Then, quietly: “Fine. You want answers? Then listen.”

He pulled a key from his pocket and unlocked a small door at the back of the shop. Behind it was a narrow staircase leading down into darkness. The air grew colder as we descended, the walls lined with more books—older, more fragile, their spines crumbling. At the bottom, a single lamp flickered to life, revealing a circular chamber. In the center stood a pedestal, and upon it rested a single object: a silver locket, its surface etched with the same symbols from the red books.

Elias picked it up. “This is yours.”

“Mine?”

“Not yours, exactly. Yours to keep. Yours to lose.”

I reached for it, but he pulled it back. “There’s a price.”

“What price?”

“Memory. You take this, you forget. And when you forget, they come for you.”

“Who?”

“The ones who own the names.”

I should have run. I should have screamed. But the locket was cold against my palm, and for the first time in years, I felt something like peace.

Elias watched me, his expression unreadable. “Do you want it?”

I closed my fingers around it.

The moment I did, the world tilted. The chamber dissolved into light, and then—

I was standing in my apartment, the morning sun streaming through the curtains. The locket was gone. The red books were gone. The bookshop was gone.

And I was alone.

---

I spent the next three days walking the streets, my mind a blank slate. I had no memory of the bookshop. No memory of Elias. No memory of the locket. Only the faintest echo of a name on my tongue—*Elias Voss*—and the certainty that I had been given something I wasn’t meant to keep.

On the fourth day, I found myself back in front of *The Last Chapter*. The door was open. Inside, Elias sat at the counter, his head bowed, his hands empty.

He looked up as I entered. “You came back.”

“I had to.”

He smiled, but it wasn’t a happy smile. “Of course you did.”

I reached into my pocket. The locket was there, warm against my skin. “I want it back.”

Elias didn’t move. “You don’t understand. Once you take it, you can’t give it back.”

“I don’t care.”

He sighed, as if I were a child making a terrible mistake. Then he reached across the counter and pressed the locket into my palm. “Then you’ll remember. And you’ll forget. And you’ll remember again.”

I closed my fingers around it. The world spun.

When I opened my eyes, I was back in the chamber, the lamp flickering, Elias standing over me. “Welcome back.”

I sat up, my head pounding. “What the hell was that?”

“A test.”

“A test for what?”

“To see if you were brave enough to look.”

I looked down at the locket. It was still there, pulsing with a faint, silver light. “What is it?”

Elias sat beside me, his voice low. “It’s a key. To a door you don’t want to open.”

“Then why give it to me?”

“Because you were always going to find it. And because some doors should only be opened when you’re ready.”

I stared at him. “And when am I ready?”

He didn’t answer. Instead, he stood and held out a hand. “Come. There’s something I need to show you.”

I took it.

We climbed the stairs, back into the shop. The red books were gone. The shelves were bare. Elias led me to the back, where a hidden door had appeared in the wall. Behind it was a staircase, this one leading upward, not downward.

“Where does this go?” I asked.

“Somewhere you don’t want to go.”

I hesitated. Then I stepped forward.

The door creaked open.

Beyond it, the world stretched endlessly—towers of books, bridges of shadows, faces watching from the darkness. And at the center, a figure stood, its form shifting between man and something else, its voice a chorus of whispers.

“Elias,” I said, my voice trembling. “What is this place?”

He didn’t answer. He was already walking away, his back to me, his steps echoing in the empty hall.

I turned back to the figure.

It smiled.

And then it spoke.

Not in words.

In names.

---

I woke up in my apartment, the locket gone, the memory of the bookshop fading like smoke. But I knew, deep down, that I would find it again. That I would open the door again. That some things were meant to be remembered, no matter how much you tried to forget.

And so I waited.

And I waited.

And I waited.
